newsitem.title: USA: Air Force pilot missing in Arizona crash.
newsitem.headline: Air Force pilot missing in Arizona crash.

text.p: An Air Force pilot was missing Wednesday after her A-10 Thunderbolt attack aircraft crashed at a training range in southwest Arizona Tuesday night.
The Air Force said the missing pilot, Capt. Amy Lynn Svoboda, was on a routine training mission from Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona when her single-seat fighter crashed.
The crash occurred at the Barry Goldwater Training Range at about 9:30 p.m. local time.

The Air Force said the A-10, designed to destroy tanks and other armor, was carrying a variety of practice weapons, including six 25 pound training bombs that emit smoke and a small flash. Authorities said these bomb dummy units have the same ballistic characteristics as larger, live ordnance.
Also on board were six 2.75-inch air-to-ground rockets and 570 rounds of 33mm practice rounds for a gatlin gun.
Additionally, the aircraft was carrying an AIM-9 practice air-to-air missle.
Svoboda is assigned to the 355th fighter wing and has been at Davis-Monthan for about a year, Air Force officials said.

She graduated from the Air Force Academy in 1989 and trained at Reese Air Force Base in Texas. She remained there as a T-37 instructor pilot until the spring of 1996 when she transferred to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in southern Arizona for A-10 training. She was certified there as a combat ready pilot.
The jet was part of a two-aircraft mission. The other plane was not involved in the accident.
Air Force officials said they have dispatched explosives and safety experts to the scene.

The crash was the second involving an A-10 from Davis-Monthan in almost two months. In April, Capt. Craig Button, 32, inexplicably left his four-aircraft formation and veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles away (1360 km) from a training exercise.
The formation was en route to the Barry Goldwater Training Range at the time.

Button's plane crashed into a snow-covered mountain peak and it was more than three weeks before a rescue team was able to recover his body. The Air Force is still investigating the crash and trying to determine why Button broke formation.
